n0001.title: Replication crisis
n0001.gist: Across psychology, medicine and other fields, published findings often fail to reproduce, exposing flaws science is now working to fix.
n0001.question: replication crisis — why do so many published findings fail to reproduce, and what can be done? (causes and reforms)

n0002.title: Defining replication
n0002.gist: Replication, repeating a study to check its conclusions, is called science's cornerstone, yet researchers still disagree on precise definitions and on how null-hypothesis statistical testing should be read.
n0002.question: replication — what exactly does it mean and how is statistical significance defined? (definitions and testing mechanics)

n0003.title: Introducing the crisis
n0003.gist: Widespread failures to reproduce published results, most visible in psychology and medicine, threaten the credibility of scientific knowledge and gave rise to the new field of metascience.

n0010.title: What counts as replication
n0010.gist: Scholars separate narrow reproducibility, rechecking the same data, from true replication with new data, and further split replication into direct, systematic and conceptual types, though no single definition is universally accepted.

n0019.title: Why replication failures are normal
n0019.gist: Failures to replicate do not prove poor rigor but reflect science's ordinary, if slow and inconsistent, process of weeding out unsupported hypotheses through significance testing.

n0022.title: Mechanics of hypothesis testing
n0022.gist: Null-hypothesis testing compares an effect size estimate against a threshold to decide significance, producing false positives and false negatives whose rates are called alpha and power respectively.

n0034.title: Power, p-values and outcomes
n0034.gist: A test's power and significance level jointly determine its four possible outcomes, and a result's p-value, often misread as the chance the null is true, instead measures how extreme the data would be if it were.

n0042.title: Emergence of the crisis
n0042.gist: A cluster of failed replications in the early 2010s, though echoing decades of earlier warnings, turned long-standing concerns about research reliability into a named crisis.
n0042.question: replication crisis — how did a long-standing problem suddenly become a named crisis in the early 2010s? (a sequence of triggering events)

n0043.title: Four precipitating failures
n0043.gist: Failed replications of social priming, extrasensory perception, and preclinical cancer studies, alongside new evidence of widespread questionable research practices, together sparked the 'crisis of confidence' in psychology.

n0050.title: Decades of earlier warnings
n0050.gist: Concerns about low replication rates, publication bias and weak statistical power had already been raised repeatedly from the late 1950s through the 1990s, long before the term 'replication crisis' existed.

n0055.title: Evidence across disciplines
n0055.gist: Large-scale replication projects in psychology, medicine, cancer biology, economics and other fields consistently find that only about a third to two-thirds of published results reproduce.
n0055.question: replication rates — how often do published findings actually replicate across different fields? (several large studies)

n0056.title: Psychology's low power problem
n0056.gist: Psychology sits at the center of the crisis because many of its subfields have long run on studies with chronically low statistical power, a structural weakness identified as early as 1962.

n0061.title: Large psychology replication projects
n0061.gist: Systematic replication projects found only 36 to 62 percent of psychology and behavioral-science findings reproduced, with effect sizes shrinking and failures occurring consistently rather than depending on sample differences.

n0066.title: Medicine and cancer biology
n0066.gist: Landmark medical and cancer studies replicate at strikingly low rates, as low as 11 to 25 percent in preclinical oncology, with effect sizes shrinking by roughly 85 percent on replication.

n0069.title: Nutrition, economics, water management
n0069.gist: Nutrition science, economics, and water-resource research all show inflated or barely reproducible effects, with one study finding fewer than 7 percent of water-management articles could even be checked.

n0079.title: Large language model research
n0079.gist: The rapid rise of large language models after 2022 created new reproducibility problems, since closed, constantly updated systems, undisclosed training data, and data leakage make findings about them hard to verify or repeat.
n0079.sourceHeading: In research on and with large language models

n0086.title: Surveys of researcher experience
n0086.gist: Surveys show most scientists have personally failed to reproduce results, including their own, yet still trust published literature, while nonreplicable papers tend to be cited more, not less, over time.

n0091.title: Causes of the crisis
n0091.gist: Historical pressures, flawed publication incentives, researcher degrees of freedom, low statistical power, and context sensitivity jointly explain why so many results fail to reproduce.
n0091.question: replication crisis — what are the root causes behind so many irreproducible findings? (several linked causes)

n0092.title: Historical and sociological roots
n0092.gist: Science's explosive growth, its commodification by funding pressures, and confusion between the codes of science, media, and the economy are longstanding structural forces behind declining research quality.

n0100.title: Publication system failures
n0100.gist: Journals overwhelmingly favor positive, significant results, hiding a 'file drawer' of unpublished null findings and allowing a high share of false positives to dominate the literature.
n0100.sourceHeading: Problems with the publication system in science

n0107.title: Mathematical and reporting errors
n0107.gist: A notable share of published statistics, even in top journals, contain outright mathematical errors or mismatched tests, often from careless typesetting or misapplied comparisons rather than fraud.

n0112.title: Publish-or-perish incentives
n0112.gist: Career pressure to publish in prestigious journals pushes researchers toward strategies that make results look publishable, misaligning individual incentives with science's collective goal of truth.

n0119.title: Weak reporting standards
n0119.gist: Many papers omit the detailed protocols, reagents, or data needed for others to redo the work, and a bias in how scientists interpret null versus non-null results can let bad evidence accumulate unchecked.

n0125.title: Questionable research practices
n0125.gist: Exploiting flexible choices in design and analysis, such as selective reporting, HARKing, and data dredging, inflates false positive rates, and surveys suggest most researchers admit to at least one such practice.

n0136.title: Low statistical power
n0136.gist: Psychology, neuroscience and economics studies typically run at only 18 to 36 percent statistical power, far below the 80 percent considered adequate, mathematically guaranteeing low replication rates.

n0145.title: Inflated effect size estimates
n0145.gist: Because only statistically significant results from small, noisy studies get published, the effect sizes that do appear in print are systematically inflated compared to a study's true underlying effect.

n0151.title: Meta-analysis and p-hacking
n0151.gist: Meta-analyses can be skewed by a single bad study or an unreliable 'fail-safe number', while flexible analysis choices, multiple testing, and optional stopping let researchers manufacture small p-values even when nothing is true.

n0169.title: Heterogeneity across studies
n0169.gist: Even exact replications of the same effect often diverge hugely because of hidden moderating factors, with a typical heterogeneity measure around 74 percent, meaning similar effect sizes should not even be expected.

n0176.title: Context, probability and testing logic
n0176.gist: Beyond incentives, deeper statistical and philosophical problems, context sensitivity, Bayesian reasoning about priors, and flaws in null-hypothesis logic itself, explain why many results cannot be expected to replicate.
n0176.question: replication failure — what deeper statistical and logical reasons make non-replication likely even without misconduct? (three arguments)

n0177.title: Context sensitivity
n0177.gist: Psychological effects often depend on hidden contextual factors, and studies show that effects rated as more context-sensitive are significantly less likely to replicate across different times, places or samples.

n0182.title: A Bayesian account
n0182.gist: Rejecting the null hypothesis at the 5 percent level does not mean the alternative is 95 percent likely to be true; under Bayes' theorem, a low prior probability or weak statistical power can make replication unlikely even for a genuine positive result.

n0190.title: Flaws in null-hypothesis testing
n0190.gist: In 'soft' sciences where almost any two variables correlate somewhat, rejecting the null hypothesis barely distinguishes among many rival explanations, and since most tested hypotheses may be false to begin with, a large share of positive results are expected to be false positives regardless of fraud.

n0206.title: Responses and reforms
n0206.gist: In response, scientists have pushed for a 'credibility revolution', more transparent methods, pre-registration, stricter significance thresholds, larger samples, and organized replication efforts.
n0206.question: replication crisis — what reforms are scientists adopting to make research more trustworthy? (a set of institutional and statistical reforms)

n0207.title: Academic and public reaction
n0207.gist: A public dispute, where a prominent psychologist attacked replication critics as 'methodological terrorists' and was rebuffed by a statistician, illustrates how contested the crisis's reception has been within academia itself, even as the German public largely sees replication efforts as quality control.

n0211.title: Toward a credibility revolution
n0211.gist: Researchers argue the crisis has spurred a 'credibility revolution' emphasizing transparency, pre-registration, and stronger evidence standards, alongside Ioannidis's parallel call to make clinical research more patient-centered and useful.

n0218.title: Reforming publishing practices
n0218.gist: Journals have adopted clearer methodology reporting, result-blind peer review that judges studies before results are known, and pre-registration of methods, all aimed at curbing publication bias and questionable practices.

n0234.title: Tracking and statistical fixes
n0234.gist: Proposed fixes include digital tools to track replication attempts, lowering the conventional significance threshold from p<0.05 to p<0.005, and better communicating the false-positive risk behind any p-value.
n0234.sourceHeading: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications

n0247.title: Larger samples and organized efforts
n0247.gist: Reformers call for larger sample sizes to counter overfitting and inflated effects, plus coordinated funding, replication databases, and large multi-lab collaborations that pool resources across countries and disciplines.

n0270.title: Rethinking the scientific approach
n0270.gist: Some argue the deeper fix is not more replication but triangulation across methods, treating psychological systems as complex and interdependent rather than linear, and using replication to actively revise and strengthen theories.

n0286.title: Open data and repositories
n0286.gist: Open data, open-source software, and public repositories like the Open Science Framework aim to make reanalysis possible, though this can expose careful researchers disproportionately to criticism when errors are found.
